newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: OUTLOOK-Pakistan seen importing cotton in first half 1997.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK-Pakistan seen importing cotton in first half 1997.

text.p: Pakistan's cotton crop has fallen short of expectations and analysts say half a million 480-lb bales will have to be imported in the first half of 1997 to meet demand from quality-conscious textile mills.

"Textile mills need 500,000 bales of imported cotton by June as the local cotton, lacking strength and staple length, is not liked by reputed mills," Maqbool Sadiq, chairman of the private Karachi Cotton Association (KCA), told Reuters.
Broker Nasim Usman said the crop would yield 8.5-8.7 million 375-lb bales in 1996/97 (July-June), compared to an official target of 10 million and production of 9.94 million in 1995/96.
"The shortfall in the crop and lack of good-quality cotton are the main reasons for an estimated import of half a million bales of cotton by June," Usman said.
Traders had already imported 80,630 bales from Central Asia in the fiscal year that began in July.
"But traders are now facing difficulty in importing cotton from the Central Asian states due to a delay in shipments, maybe due to a shortage or high prices abroad," Sadiq said.

Usman said Central Asian producers had oversold stocks without assessing the crop size or taking into account high world prices. "The crop seems to be short in Central Asia and exporters there are not shipping consignments on time," he said.

The shortage of quality cotton pushed the price of MNH-93 up to 2,618.50 rupees ($65) per maund (37.32 kg) on Thursday in local markets. "Prices are likely to rise further on mill demand and delay in shipment from Central Asia," Usman said.
Broker Kishin Chand said soaring local prices had dampened hopes of exporters who had planned to export $600 million of cotton in 1996/97, compared to $504.6 million in 1995/96.
Dealers had registered only 14,757 375-lb bales of cotton with the state-run Export Promotion Bureau by November 27, compared to 2.568 million bales at the same time last year.
Exporters had actually shipped only 2,005 bales by October 28 compared to 27,563 a year earlier, a KCA spokesman said.
Aijazuddin Ghauri, secretary of the Pakistan Cotton Ginners Association, said 5.605 million bales had arrived at ginneries by November, compared to 5.431 million in the year-ago period.
Textile mills had bought 4.028 million bales by November, against 3.544 million in the year-ago period, encouraged by rising international demand for cotton yarn, Ghauri said.

Chand said textile mills would be able to reap healthy profits thanks to higher yarn prices abroad. Foreign exchange earnings from yarn were likely to be much higher than the $600 million that had been envisaged from raw cotton exports.
An official at the All Pakistan Textile Mills Association (APTMA) said mills would probably require some 9.5 million bales in 1996/97, compared to about 8.9 million in 1995/96.
In October, APTMA demanded duty-free import of at least one million bales of cotton to compensate for the crop shortfall.
Last month the government withdrew a five percent customs duty on cotton imports to boost the textile sector and slashed regulatory duties on synthetic fibre imports.

APTMA says consumption will rise because 800,000 out of two million idle spindles are likely to be reactivated to meet export demand for yarn. Pakistan's textile mills have an installed capacity of 8.8 million spindles.
